section: Key Challenge: Relational Integrity & Operational Data Noise
text:
Key Challenge: Relational Integrity & Operational Data Noise

The Technical Hurdle: Raw e-commerce export tables contained over 100,000 unindexed transaction rows spread across 8 separate datasets. Initial pipeline attempts faced join fan-out issues (duplicate row counts when joining item-level prices with order-level payments) and foreign key mismatches due to unmapped category translation tables.
The Solution: Engineered a strict normalized relational schema in PostgreSQL, establishing primary/foreign key constraints and utilizing COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) to prevent aggregation inflation. Isolated operational noise by filtering explicitly for completed delivery states (order_status = 'delivered'), ensuring that revenue calculations reflected actual cash flow.

title: Relational Database Engineering & E-Commerce SQL Analytics
text:
README

Executive Summary
This project analyzes 96,478 delivered orders totaling $13.2M+ in gross revenue from a major Brazilian e-commerce marketplace. Operating as the Lead Data Analyst, I designed the relational database architecture in PostgreSQL (via VS Code), managed bulk data ingestion across 8 interconnected tables, and authored structured analytical queries to answer executive-level business questions.
The analysis provides clear visibility into platform revenue drivers, payment processing habits, seasonal growth spikes, and the severe customer rating penalties caused by fulfillment delays.



Core Business Questions & Key Insights

1. What is the baseline revenue volume and top product category performance?

Method: Multi-table JOINs connecting item pricing, product specs, and English translation mappings, aggregated by revenue volume.
Insight: Total platform gross revenue reached $13,221,498.11 across 96,478 completed orders, with an average item price of $119.98. health_beauty took the #1 category spot ($1.26M revenue across 8,836 orders), followed closely by watches_gifts ($1.20M) and bed_bath_table ($1.04M).



2. How do customers pay, and what are the credit card financing habits?

Method: Group aggregations and mean installment calculations on transaction methods.
Insight: Credit Cards dominate the platform, driving 76.2% of all transactions and $12.54M in total value. Furthermore, credit card customers choose an average of 3.5 installments, demonstrating that flexible financing options are critical for conversion in this market. Cash-based Boleto payments ranked second ($2.87M).



3. How severely do fulfillment delays harm customer satisfaction?

Method: Conditional logic (CASE WHEN) flagging orders delivered past their estimated delivery date, joined with customer review scores.
Insight: On-time orders (88,163 orders) maintained a high average satisfaction rating of 4.29 / 5.00. However, late orders (7,661 orders) suffered a steep rating collapse to 2.57 / 5.00—a massive 1.72-star drop. While late deliveries accounted for only ~8% of total volume, they disproportionately degraded brand trust.



4. How can we segment customers by lifetime monetary value?

Method: Common Table Expression (CTE) paired with PostgreSQL Window Functions (NTILE(4)).
Insight: Segmented the entire customer base into 4 distinct spend quartiles. Isolated the top 25% VIP spenders (Quartile 1) and identified high-value outliers, including a top single customer generating $13,664.08 in total order volume.

title: Sustainability Analytics & Business Intelligence
section: Key Challenge: Feature Confounding & Global Data Complexity
text:
Key Challenge: Feature Confounding & Global Data Complexity

The Technical Hurdle: Modeling relationships between socioeconomic development and ecological impact introduced significant feature overlap. Variables such as Human Development Index (HDI), income classification, and economic indicators captured similar underlying patterns, creating multicollinearity that threatened model interpretability.
The Solution: I redesigned the analytical workflow by separating predictive modeling from exploratory visualization. Correlated socioeconomic variables were evaluated independently during statistical modeling, while economic classifications were preserved for dashboard segmentation. This maintained strong predictive performance (\(R^2 = 0.78\)) while producing a clearer analytical framework.

title: Sustainability Analytics & Business Intelligence
text:
README

Executive Summary
How can societies continue economic development without exceeding the planet’s ecological capacity?
This project analyzes global ecological footprint trends by combining socioeconomic indicators, resource consumption metrics, and biocapacity measurements across 182 countries.
Using Python-based data engineering workflows and interactive Tableau deployment, this analysis investigates how economic development patterns influence environmental demand and identifies the primary drivers behind global ecological overshoot.
The project integrates statistical preprocessing, missing-data management, exploratory analysis, and business intelligence visualization to transform complex sustainability datasets into accessible decision-support tools.
The Core Finding: Global ecological deficits are driven primarily by carbon-intensive infrastructure and consumption patterns, rather than simple land resource scarcity. While many biological resource categories remain near equilibrium, fossil-fuel-driven economic systems create the largest imbalance between human demand and Earth’s regenerative capacity.

title: Sustainability Analytics & Business Intelligence
text:
The Missing Data Challenge
The Global Footprint Network dataset contained incomplete socioeconomic records across countries, creating challenges for consistent global comparison.
The Problem: Removing incomplete observations would disproportionately exclude countries with limited reporting infrastructure, introducing geographic bias into downstream analysis.
The Solution: I developed a regional median imputation workflow that preserved global coverage while maintaining realistic socioeconomic distributions.
The pipeline:

Validated missing-value patterns across global records
Grouped observations by geographic region
Applied regional statistical baselines for missing values
Preserved country-level representation for visualization and modeling

title: Sustainability Analytics & Business Intelligence
text:
Resolving Multicollinearity in Socioeconomic Indicators
Initial modeling revealed strong relationships between economic classification variables and human development measurements.
HDI demonstrated predictive significance independently, but introducing overlapping categorical variables reduced interpretability due to shared variance.
The Analytical Fix:

Removed redundant predictors during regression modeling
Evaluated economic variables independently
Used categorical classifications primarily for visualization
Preserved interpretability for stakeholder communication

title: Statistical Analysis & Predictive Modeling
section: Key Challenge: Non-Linear Skew & Spatial Decoupling
text:
Key Challenge: Non-Linear Skew & Spatial Decoupling

The Technical Hurdle: Initial predictive modeling struggled heavily with the right-skewed nature of fisheries catch data, yielding an \(R^2\) of just 0.076 due to extreme data volatility and high-leverage catching anomalies. While a log-transformation was necessary, early base-R data aggregation pipelines inadvertently decoupled the spatial alignment of the dataset, causing the model to completely lose the signal of environmental predictors (\(R^2 = \textbf{0.015}\)).
The Solution: I migrated the data pipeline to a unified tidyverse aggregation framework that precisely synchronized spatial and environmental metrics using individual haul signatures. Refitting the log-transformed response with a quadratic term for ocean depth unlocked the true dynamics of the ecosystem, expanding the model’s explanatory power to 39.6%. This architectural fix mathematically isolated both an explicit parabolic depth preference boundary and an acute negative population response to rising bottom temperatures.

title: Statistical Analysis & Predictive Modeling
text:
README

Executive Summary
In 2021, NOAA Fisheries resumed data collection after global pandemic restrictions halted field surveys for two years. They discovered that during that data blackout, over 10 billion snow crabs had vanished from the Eastern Bering Sea, effectively wiping out a historically stable population and crippling a lucrative $150M annual fishery, with no initial explanation.
This project uses multivariate regression, discriminant analysis, and 2D kernel density estimation on historical NOAA bottom-trawl survey data (1975–2018) to “back-cast” the population’s likely location during the unmonitored 2019 season, a summer in which the predicted area experienced a record breaking marine heatwave.
The Core Finding: The analysis reveals a mathematical “Climate Trap.” Decadal trends show the population steadily migrating northwest toward a structural dead-end. When the heatwave struck, the crabs were geographically bottlenecked in the shallow waters of Bristol Bay—bound by a strict, parabolic depth requirement and land barriers, leaving them with zero escape routes to cooler, deeper water.



Core Research Questions & Key Insights

1. What environmental factors dictate catch success?

Method: Multivariate Linear Regression utilizing log-transformed Catch Per Unit Effort (CPUE) and quadratic features for bathymetric depth.
Insight: Population density is tightly bound to a non-linear “Goldilocks Zone” for depth. Both bottom depth and the quadratic term are ultra-significant. Rising bottom temperatures show an acute, crushing negative impact on density, proving that cold-acclimated crabs actively flee warming waters.



2. Do environmental niches diverge by sex?

Method: Linear & Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (LDA/QDA).
Insight: Classifiers yielded high cross-validated test error rates (~39.6% for QDA), revealing that males and females share an inseparable fundamental environmental niche. However, secondary spatial mapping uncovered behavioral segregation: females cluster tightly along deep northwestern shelf margins for egg preservation, whereas males disperse widely southeast to mitigate territorial aggression.



3. Can we track historical migration to locate the population during the data gap?

Method: 2D Kernel Density Estimation paired with joint linear vector modeling over time.
Insight: The Year variable alone explains 50.6% of longitudinal variance and 44.4% of latitudinal variance. The population has followed a remarkably rigid, statistically ironclad trajectory northwest for decades.

title: Statistical Analysis & Predictive Modeling
text: Data Engineering & Pipeline Refactoring

title: Statistical Analysis & Predictive Modeling
text:
The Data Alignment Challenge
The raw NOAA dataset spans \(n = 17,927\) individual specimen observations. Early modeling attempts in base R yielded a broken model with an \(R^2\) of just 1.5%, indicating that the environment had no statistical relationship with crab location.
The Bug: Fragmented base-R aggregate() and cbind() scripts decoupled row synchronization across features. The model was inadvertently mapping the catch numbers of Haul A to the ocean depths of Haul B.
The Fix: Migrating to a unified, declarative tidyverse pipeline forced all geospatial, biological, and thermal features to collapse simultaneously by their unique haul signatures:
Upon executing this fix, the true ecological signals instantly locked into place, expanding the model’s explanatory power from 1.5% to 39.6% (F=773.7,p<2.2×10−16).

title: Statistical Analysis & Predictive Modeling
text:
The Back-Casting Projection (The Climate Trap)
By modeling the decadal centroid shift of the population, our joint linear framework projected the population’s coordinates directly into the unmonitored 2019 horizon.
Overlaying these predicted coordinates onto NOAA’s 2019 thermal anomaly maps reveals the tragedy:
The predictive engine places the population squarely within the shallow, enclosed pocket of Bristol Bay. Hemmed in by land to the north and unable to cross the western shelf edge due to strict parabolic depth limitations, the population was physically cornered. Forced into a geographic bottleneck experiencing peak marine heatwave temperatures, the cold-acclimated species suffered a cataclysmic, metabolic-driven mass mortality event.

Create Total Success Metric (Haul Aggregation)

# Safely aggregate all physical factors by Year and Haul simultaneously
haul_df <- snowcrab_raw %>%
  group_by(year, haul) %>%
  summarize(
    CPUE = sum(cpue, na.rm = TRUE),
    lat = mean(latitude, na.rm = TRUE),
    long = mean(longitude, na.rm = TRUE),
    bottom_depth = mean(bottom_depth, na.rm = TRUE),
    surface_temp = mean(surface_temperature, na.rm = TRUE),
    bottom_temp = mean(bottom_temperature, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(Haul_ID = row_number()) %>%
  dplyr::select(Haul_ID, Year = year, Haul_Num = haul, CPUE, lat, long, bottom_depth, surface_temp, bottom_temp)

Classification Analysis

snowcrab_class <- snowcrab %>%
  mutate(sex = as.numeric(sex))

n <- nrow(snowcrab_class)
set.seed(8)
train_idx <- sample(n, round(n * 0.8, 0))
test_idx  <- setdiff(1:n, train_idx)

train_set <- snowcrab_class[train_idx, ]
test_set <- snowcrab_class[test_idx, ]

# Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
lda.fit <- lda(sex ~ ., data = train_set)
lda.pred <- predict(lda.fit, test_set)
table(Predicted = lda.pred$class, Actual = test_set$sex)

         Actual
Predicted    1    2

        2 1143 1766

lda.test.error <- mean(lda.pred$class != test_set$sex)
print(paste("LDA Test Error:", round(lda.test.error, 4)))

# Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA)

qda.pred <- predict(qda.fit, test_set)

5-Fold Cross Validation

set.seed(12)
k <- 5
folds <- sample(1:k, nrow(snowcrab_class), replace = TRUE)

lda.cv.errors <- rep(0, k)
qda.cv.errors <- rep(0, k)

for (i in 1:k) {
  train_fold <- snowcrab_class[folds != i, ]
  test_fold  <- snowcrab_class[folds == i, ]
  
  # LDA
  lda.f <- lda(sex ~ ., data = train_fold)
  lda.p <- predict(lda.f, test_fold)
  lda.cv.errors[i] <- mean(lda.p$class != test_fold$sex)
  
  # QDA
  qda.f <- qda(sex ~ ., data = train_fold)
  qda.p <- predict(qda.f, test_fold)
  qda.cv.errors[i] <- mean(qda.p$class != test_fold$sex)
}

# Aggregating Average Trajectory Coordinates safely

    lat = mean(lat, na.rm = TRUE)
